summary: Fred Atkins, a twenty-year-old billiard-marker, bookmaker's clerk and music-hall comedian, was introduced into the circle by Maurice Schwabe in November 1892 and taken to Paris by Wilde as nominal 'private secretary.' The plea alleged sexual acts there; Atkins on oath denied any impropriety with Wilde while describing Schwabe in Wilde's bed. His credibility collapsed on recall when he was proved to have lied about a Rochester Row blackmail arrest, and the jury acquitted Wilde on every Atkins count.

disputed.claim: that Wilde solicited and committed acts of gross indecency with Frederick Atkins at 29 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris, on 20 November 1892
disputed.asserted_by: Queensberry's plea of justification (filed 30 March 1895); Crown indictment counts in Regina v. Wilde and Taylor (1895); circumstantially, Mary Applegate's testimony about the sheets at Osnaburgh Street (Hyde p. 211)
disputed.disputed_by: Atkins's own sworn testimony ('Did any impropriety ever take place between you and Mr. Wilde?—Never.'); Wilde's denials on oath at the libel trial; the jury's not-guilty verdict on the Atkins counts, 1 May 1895
disputed.grounds: the witness was exposed as a perjurer mid-trial (Rochester Row charge-sheet produced; 'Leave the box' — Hyde pp. 217-218) and both prosecution and defence positions on Atkins failed; Hyde's introduction records the jury 'found the prisoners not guilty on the charges relating to Atkins' (p. 74)

sources.quote: Examination continued—I got back to the rooms very late. Mr. Wilde was in bed. I went into his room and had something to drink. A man of about twenty-two years of age was in bed with Mr. Wilde. It was Schwabe. I went to bed by myself. Before I got out of bed in the morning Mr. Wilde came into my room. That was about nine o'clock. He talked about the Moulin Rouge and I told him that I had enjoyed myself. Mr. Wilde then said to me, "Shall I come into bed with you?" I replied that it was time to get up. Mr. Wilde did not get into bed with me.
sources.context: Fred Atkins's examination-in-chief on the Paris trip, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895
sources.supports: Atkins's own account of the Paris nights: an invitation declined, no act with Wilde described

sources.quote: And that the said Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde on the twentieth day of November in the year of our Lord One thousand eight hundred and ninety-two at a house situate at 29 Boulevard des Capucines in Paris in the Republic of France did solicit and incite one Frederick Atkins to commit sodomy and other acts of gross indecency and immorality with him the said Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde and did then and there commit the said other acts of gross indecency and immorality with the said Frederick Atkins.

sources.quote: Had I cared to show that the Crown witnesses — the three most important — had been carefully coached by your father and his solicitors, not in reticences merely, but in assertions, in the absolute transference, deliberate, plotted, and rehearsed, of the actions and doings of someone else on to me, I could have had each one of them dismissed from the box by the Judge, more summarily than even wretched perjured Atkins was.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas (De Profundis), Reading Prison, January-March 1897; the editors' note on the page records that the judge's summing-up called Atkins 'a most reckless, unreliable, unscrupulous, and untruthful witness' and that Wilde 'was acquitted of the charges brought in respect of this witness' (p. 714 n 1)
sources.supports: Wilde's retrospective characterization ('wretched perjured Atkins') and his counter-claim that the testimony transferred someone else's doings onto him
